        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run manually) to get everything set up.  
I’ll walk through what you need to do locally, what files I’m generating for you, and the exact git commands to finish the job.

> ⚠️ **Important** – I don’t have the ability to actually clone or push to your repo, so you’ll need to run the commands yourself.  
> If you hit an error, let me know the exact message and I’ll help troubleshoot.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL accordingly.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Files

### 2.1 Inspect the Project Structure

Run a quick check to see what the entry point looks like:

```bash
cat package.json | grep -E '"main"|\"start\"' -A 5
```

Typical output will look something like:

```json
{
  "name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "src/index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node src/index.js"
  },
  ...
}
```

If the `main` field points to `src/index.js`, that’s our entry point.  
If it’s missing, look for a script called `"start"` or a file named `app.js`.

> **Tip:** If the repo contains a `Dockerfile` already, back it up first (`mv Dockerfile Dockerfile.bak`) before overwriting.

### 2.2 Create/Update the Dockerfile

Create a new `Dockerfile` (or overwrite the existing one):

```bash
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
# Use official lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
EXPOSE 3000

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy rest of the source
COPY . .

# Default command
CMD [ "npm", "start" ]
EOF
```

> Adjust the base image (`node:18-alpine`) or the exposed port (`3000`) if your app uses a different version or port.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a `k8s/deployment.yaml` (create the folder if it doesn’t exist):

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
cat > k8s/deployment.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/your-github-username/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update later
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP as needed
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # Exposed externally
    targetPort: 3000          # Matches containerPort above
EOF
```

> Replace `ghcr.io/your-github-username/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual registry/image you’ll push to (see section 3).

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a workflow file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > .github/workflows/docker-build.yml <<'EOF'
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed for GHCR

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up QEMU
      uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }},ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
EOF
```

> *Why this workflow?*  
> • Uses the built‑in `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> • Builds multi‑arch images via Buildx.  
> • Caches layers to speed up subsequent builds.  
> • Tags both a SHA‑specific tag and `latest`.  

> If you prefer Docker Hub, change the login action and tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add All Changes to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you backed up an old Dockerfile, you may want to keep it in the repo as `Dockerfile.old` or delete it after verifying the new one works.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "CI/CD: Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next push to `main`.  
> Check the “Actions” tab in your repo to confirm the build succeeded.

---

## 🎉 What Happens Next?

1. **GitHub Actions** builds a Docker image and pushes it to `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome`.
2. Your **Kubernetes YAML** references that image; you can deploy it with:

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/
   ```

3. Once deployed, the service will expose your app (via LoadBalancer or NodePort).  
   Verify with `kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service`.

---

### Need Help Running These Commands?

If you run into any errors (e.g., authentication failures, build failures), paste the exact error log here and I’ll help debug. Happy coding!
